about: Lesson F7 (f07-microgrids). Prairie Campus, its county hospital and the village are fictional; every load, size and fuel figure is illustrative. The solar shapes are real: assets/learn/data/town_year.json (SPP's 2025 hourly solar from EIA-930), turned into output per kW of panels with LX.townProfile (assets/learn/components/profiles.js, method 'scale'): the campus windows with monthlyCF (EIA's 2025 monthly capacity factors), the village's average day with the annual 24.0% only (the mean of each hour over 2025). _tests/learn/test_f07-microgrids.js recomputes them. The research text (realWorld) is approved excerpt wording, word for word (E8.2, E8.7, E9.1-E9.3).

parts.name: Grid feeder
parts.note: The utility's distribution line that brings grid power to the campus.

parts.name: Switch to the grid
parts.note: The [[point-of-common-coupling|point of common coupling]]: the one place the campus meets the grid. Opening it islands the campus.

parts.name: Controller
parts.note: Decides when to island, which sources run and which loads stay on.

parts.name: Solar panels, 600 kW
parts.note: Their [[inverter|inverters]] are [[grid-following|grid-following]]: they follow a voltage that something else sets, so they cannot start an island alone.

parts.name: Battery, 500 kW and 2,000 kWh
parts.note: Its [[grid-forming|grid-forming]] inverter is designed to start the island and set its voltage and frequency.

parts.name: Diesel generator, 400 kW
parts.note: Fuel for 24 hours at full power. Once started, it can form an island too.

parts.name: Water and heating plant, 100 kW
parts.note: Critical too: the hospital needs water and heat.

parts.name: Dorms, 250 kW
parts.note: Can go dark in an emergency, if they must.

parts.name: Classrooms and labs, 550 kW
parts.note: The largest load, and the first to shed.

texts.solarOff: Ordinary grid-connected solar [[inverter|inverters]] must stop feeding a grid section that has been cut off, so a downed line stays safe for repair crews.
texts.formSolar: Solar inverters are [[grid-following|grid-following]]: they need a voltage to follow. Pick something that can form the island.
texts.formBattery: The battery's [[grid-forming|grid-forming]] inverter sets the island's voltage and frequency, and the solar inverters follow it. The controller picks up the hospital and the water plant first.
texts.formGen: Once it has started, the generator sets the island's voltage and frequency, and the solar inverters follow it. The controller picks up the hospital and the water plant first.
texts.keepCritical: The hospital and the water plant are critical: the hospital needs water and heat. Switch both back on.
texts.boundary: We assume the switching and the start succeed: this lesson checks power and energy, not a seamless changeover.
texts.villageToy: Toy check: one average day; the battery can give any power the village needs, so only stored energy is tested, not cloudy days.

flow.title: When the grid goes down
flow.lede: Four questions decide what stays lit. Trace a case through them.

q1.t: Can it open a switch and run alone?

traces.label: A home with rooftop solar only
traces.text: An ordinary grid-connected inverter has no switch to run alone, so it stops and the home goes dark.

traces.label: The village
traces.text: There is no grid to lose: the village runs as an island every day, so only power and energy matter.

kinds.title: Kinds of microgrid
kinds.caption: The first four rows follow DOE's microgrid overview (2019); the village row follows the World Bank's 2025 energy-access report.

rows.name: Commercial or industrial
rows.why: Cut costs while connected; backup power in an outage

rows.name: Facility, such as a campus
rows.why: Link critical facilities and their equipment

rows.name: Rural community or island
rows.why: Burn less imported fuel; more resilience

cards.text: A campus with solar, a battery, a generator, a controller and one switch to the grid
cards.why: Loads and sources inside one boundary, run as one unit, and able to island.

cards.text: A village's panels, batteries and wires, with no grid connection at all
cards.why: An isolated microgrid: it runs as an island all the time.

cards.text: A house with rooftop solar and an ordinary grid-connected inverter
cards.why: It cannot run alone: its inverter stops when the grid does.

cards.text: A standby generator on its own, with no controller, that starts after the grid fails
cards.why: Backup only: nothing runs sources and loads as one unit. A microgrid can still serve one building.

cards.text: A wind farm connected to the transmission grid
cards.why: A power plant that sells to the grid; it serves no local loads of its own.

cards.text: An island's diesel generators, wind turbines and batteries, with no link to a mainland
cards.why: A whole small grid run as one unit, isolated from any larger one.

facts.what: Average time a U.S. customer was without power, major events included, at utilities that report by the IEEE method: 269.2 minutes in 2025 and 662.6 minutes in 2024.
facts.source: EIA, Electric Power Annual, Table 11.1 (IEEE method, all events)

facts.what: Operating U.S. microgrids in DOE's Microgrid Installation Database when it launched, and their total capacity.
People without electricity in 2023. Mini-grids and off-grid solar are among the ways to reach them.
